reason: E3 directly demonstrates that ~55 ms flash heating yields uniform single-phase HEA nanoparticles, supporting the baseline and kinetic trapping premise. E1 provides a model linking limited atomic mobility to random mixing and notes that extended mobility can cause segregation, supporting the diffusion-limited mechanism. E2 is only loosely related, discussing thermal decomposition and liquid bead formation but not dwell-time effects or kinetic trapping, leaving the specific role of dwell time and the extension to noble metals partially supported.
premises: Ultrafast heating/cooling can produce single-phase solid-solution HEA nanoparticles from mixed precursors
Limited atomic mobility during synthesis kinetically traps a random, high-entropy configuration
Extending high-temperature dwell time increases atomic diffusion, enabling local ordering and phase separation
The kinetic trapping mechanism applies to noble metal systems with >5 elements under extreme thermal conditions
A minimal dwell time (~55 ms) is sufficient to freeze a uniform single-phase state
